standard.title: Explain civic participation methods
standard.description: explain the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explained methods and strategies for civic participation at Year 7 level (AC9HC7S04). The gap this descriptor fills is explaining those methods in the context of decision-making — not just naming strategies but explaining the reasoning behind choosing particular strategies for particular civic aims, and the links between democratic societies, active citizenship and global citizenship.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation, including active citizenship strategies, the links between democracy and active and global citizenship, and the methods used to take civic action at different scales.

nodes.label: Active citizenship strategies and their purposes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how active citizenship strategies may contribute to informed and positive change, explaining the purpose of different strategies in building a democratically cohesive society.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two active citizenship strategies and explain how each contributes to democratic participation or positive civic change.
nodes.typical_width: Describe a range of active citizenship strategies — including campaigning, lobbying, community organising, public advocacy, direct action and participation in formal democratic processes — and explain how each can contribute to informed and positive change and to building a democratically cohesive society, drawing on examples such as stopping whaling or reducing carbon emissions.
wider: Investigate a successful civic campaign in Australia and analyse which active citizenship strategies were used, why those strategies were chosen and what made them effective

Compare active citizenship strategies across different civic contexts — environmental campaigns, social justice movements, community advocacy — examining whether the same strategies transfer across contexts
Investigate how digital tools and social media have created new active citizenship strategies and changed the landscape of civic participation
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that civic participation requires strategy — that different methods suit different aims and contexts — is the prerequisite for explaining the decision-making aspect of this descriptor. A student who treats civic participation as a list of things people do cannot explain how or why particular strategies are chosen.

response_modes.reason: Students need a working repertoire of active citizenship strategies with concrete examples before they can reason about choosing between them. Invest in building that repertoire across diverse contexts.

success_criteria: Can describe at least two distinct active citizenship strategies
Can explain how each strategy contributes to civic change or democratic cohesion, not just describe what it involves

nodes.label: Democracy, active citizenship and global citizenship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the links between democratic societies, active citizenship and global citizenship at national, regional and global levels.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how active citizenship connects to democracy at one level (national, regional or global) with a specific example.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the links between democratic societies, active citizenship and global citizenship at national, regional and global levels — including how civic engagement in a democracy creates space for active citizenship, and how active citizenship can operate at scales beyond the national (e.g. citizens who protest against militaristic or authoritarian regimes or abuses of human rights in other societies).
wider: Investigate a specific example of cross-border civic action — such as international solidarity campaigns, transnational advocacy networks or diaspora political engagement — and analyse how it expresses global citizenship
Examine how global civic movements (e.g. climate strikes, human rights campaigns) connect local active citizenship to global democratic challenges
Investigate the tensions between national citizenship obligations and global citizenship responsibilities — where they align and where they conflict

response_modes.reason: The national/regional/global scale dimension is genuinely varied. Widening across all three scales prevents students from treating civic participation as only national-level.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Connecting active citizenship to global citizenship extends students' civic perspective beyond the nation-state. Width across examples at different scales builds understanding of civic participation as a genuinely multi-level practice, with real-world relevance to global issues students encounter.
success_criteria: Can explain the link between democratic society and active citizenship
Can give an example of civic participation at a level beyond the national (regional or global) and explain how it expresses active or global citizenship

nodes.label: Making decisions about civic participation strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the reasoning involved in choosing civic participation strategies — how the choice of strategy is shaped by the aim, the context and the available options.
nodes.minimum_width: For a given civic issue, explain why one particular participation strategy would be appropriate, referencing the aim and context.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation — examining how the choice of strategy depends on the civic aim, the political and legal context, the scale of the issue, the resources available and the likely audience. Apply this reasoning to real or hypothetical civic scenarios.
wider: Analyse a case where a civic group had to choose between different participation strategies (e.g. legal challenge vs direct action vs political lobbying) and evaluate the reasoning behind the choice made
Investigate how civic participation strategies differ in authoritarian versus democratic contexts — examining what strategies are available when formal democratic channels are restricted or absent
Develop and justify a civic participation plan for a current issue, explaining each strategic decision with reference to aim, context and likely effect

response_modes.reason: This node integrates active citizenship strategies and the democracy/global citizenship links into the decision-making framework the descriptor explicitly requires. Ensure students apply reasoning — not just description — to strategic choice.

success_criteria: Can explain at least two factors that would influence the choice of civic participation strategy for a given issue
Can justify a strategic choice for a civic scenario with reference to aim and context
